title: Growing broccoli microgreens
subtitle: Mild brassica cotyledons ready to cut in 7 to 10 days
excerpt: Broccoli microgreens are among the most popular tray crops. They germinate evenly, grow steadily, and produce pale green cotyledons with a mild brassica flavour. Sow on a 25 cm tray, blackout for three days, then bring to light and cut between day 7 and 10.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard commercial microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material and tray-growing instruction.

glossaryTerms.definition: The seed leaf that emerges first when a seed germinates. In microgreen growing, the cotyledon stage is the harvest window: fully-expanded seed leaves with no true leaves yet showing.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Broccoli microgreens are an indoor, year-round crop sown on a 25 cm tray. The cycle runs 7 to 10 days from sowing to the first cut: sow, blackout for two to three days until the shoots push 3 cm, then move to light and cut with scissors when the
are fully expanded. The flavour is mild, slightly sweet brassica, with none of the sharp edge of radish or mustard.

Broccoli is a reliable first microgreen crop because it germinates uniformly and the cotyledons are easy to read at harvest. There is a clear window: open, green, and standing upright is correct; starting to wrinkle or produce the first true leaves is too late.

Light source: a south or west-facing windowsill works in the spring and summer months. In winter, a supplementary LED grow light set 15 to 20 cm above the tray and run for 14 hours a day produces more uniform cotyledons than available natural light. Broccoli microgreens grown in low winter light become pale and slightly leggy; they are still edible but less crisp.

Ambient temperature: 18 to 22°C. Broccoli germinates readily at room temperature; below 15°C the cycle slows to 12 or more days and the risk of mould on the medium surface increases during the extended blackout phase.

Day 0: sow. Dampen seed compost or coir block to field-moisture (damp to the squeeze but not dripping), fill the tray to within 1 cm of the rim, and level. Scatter broccoli seed evenly at about 15 to 20 g per 25 cm tray. Press gently to ensure seed-to-medium contact. Broccoli microgreen seed is small; a salt-shaker motion from 30 cm above the tray distributes it more evenly than a direct pour.

Days 1 to 3: blackout. Stack a second empty tray over the sown tray. A light weight on top keeps the cover flat. In the dark and under light pressure the shoots push straight upward; this is what produces the straight-stemmed, uniformly-tall cotyledons that are easier to cut clean. Check once daily from day 2. Remove the cover when the shoots are 2 to 3 cm tall.

Day 4 onward: light. Bring the tray into light. The cotyledons green up within 24 hours. Water from below by setting the growing tray inside a second tray containing 1 to 2 cm of water; allow the medium to draw moisture upward. Top-watering at this stage sends water across the surface and risks mould and
. Water once daily or when the medium feels light.

Days 7 to 10: cut. The cotyledons are ready when they are fully open, green, and standing 5 to 8 cm tall. Cut with sharp scissors 1 cm above the medium surface. A single 25 cm tray yields roughly two large handfuls of cotyledons. Use fresh or refrigerate for up to two days in a sealed container.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting the tray
attrs.intro: Common problems in broccoli microgreen trays and what causes them.

items.symptom: Stems rot and collapse at the base within the first few days
items.cause: Damping off from overwatered medium or poorly ventilated conditions.
items.fix: Bottom-water only, never top-water. Ensure the room has some airflow around the tray. Discard the affected tray and start fresh; damping off spreads quickly through a dense sowing.

items.symptom: White fuzz on the medium surface between the stems
items.cause: Surface mould on the substrate, usually from moisture on top of the growing medium.
items.fix: Switch to bottom-watering entirely. Some airflow from a small nearby fan reduces surface mould significantly. The mould is typically on the substrate, not on the stems, and the cotyledons remain safe to cut and eat.

items.symptom: Germination patchy, some areas of the tray sparse
items.cause: Uneven seed distribution, dry medium edges, or old seed stock with low viability.
items.fix: Distribute seed more evenly with a shaker motion. Ensure the medium is uniformly damp before sowing. Test new seed stock with a small germination test before committing a full tray.

items.symptom: Cotyledons yellow and fail to green up after moving to light
items.cause: Insufficient light, or blackout phase ended too soon and cotyledons still buried.
items.fix: Move to a brighter position or add a grow light. Make sure shoots are 2 to 3 cm tall before removing the blackout cover.

content.text: Use untreated broccoli seed. Standard vegetable seed may carry a fungicide coating that is not appropriate for consumption at the cotyledon stage. Microgreen suppliers sell untreated broccoli seed in larger volumes; the cost per tray is lower than buying small vegetable-seed packets.
